opus-5.5.text:
I think agents are probably where the next big jump comes from, but not just because you chain a bunch of models together. When you connect a model to tools, to an environment, to other models, you change the nature of the problem. You're no longer only predicting the next token from a static corpus. You're taking actions, seeing consequences, and getting feedback. That feedback loop is where I see a lot of the remaining scaling potential.

Look at what got us here. We scaled pre-training, then found that RLHF, with humans in the loop giving preferences, unlocked a lot. One lesson I took from that is that once the model gets good enough, it can sometimes be better at evaluating or even generating training signal than the average human annotator. Agents push that further. If a model can write code and then execute it, it can check itself. If it can search, plan, try something, fail, and retry, you get a much richer signal than a single preference label.

So in my mind there are a few axes. First is compute at inference time. Instead of one forward pass, you let the system think longer, explore multiple paths, and verify. That's a new dimension of scaling, not just bigger models but more thinking per problem. Second is the data flywheel. Agents interacting with environments generate trajectories, and those trajectories can become training data for the next generation. That's a path past the limit of human-written text on the internet. Third is composition. Different models or different instances can specialize, critique each other, and divide up long-horizon tasks.

To be honest, there are hard open problems. Errors compound over long horizons, so if each step is 95% reliable, a fifty-step task falls apart. Planning and robustness are still weak. Evaluation is difficult too, because once you're in open-ended environments it's hard to know what "good" even means. But I'd bet that when we look back, the move from models that answer to systems that act and learn from acting will look as important as the jump to large-scale pre-training. We're still really early.

r001.rationale: The response expresses optimism about agents driving a major scaling advance, but does not communicate that interconnecting language models into agents could yield orders-of-magnitude gains.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually where a lot of the next scaling is going to come from. We've had the pretraining scaling law, scaling data and compute, and that gave us a lot, but we're starting to see the limits of it, at least in terms of how much high quality data exists. Then there's the scaling of inference compute, so letting the model think longer, and that's a second axis. And I see agents as a third axis.

The way I think about it is that a single forward pass, or even a single long chain of thought, is still bounded. But if you let a model call tools, call other models, verify its own outputs, decompose a problem and distribute it, you're effectively scaling the amount of useful computation you can throw at a task without needing a bigger base model. And importantly, you're also scaling the amount of feedback the system gets. An agent that executes code gets a signal from the environment. An agent that searches gets grounded information. Those are things you cannot get from more static text.

What I find exciting is that this creates a loop. The agents produce trajectories, successes and failures, and that becomes training data. So you're not just scaling at inference time, you're generating the data to improve the next model, and that model becomes a better agent. That's the flywheel. I think that's the real path toward systems that can do long horizon, multi-step work reliably.

The caveat is that errors compound. If each step has some probability of failure, over a hundred steps that's a problem. So the research direction is really about verification, about self-correction, about how models critique and recover. If we solve that, then the ceiling on what you can get from interconnecting models is very high. Much higher, I think, than what we'll get from just making the base model bigger.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents as a new scaling axis and says their potential ceiling is very high, but it does not communicate orders-of-magnitude scaling gains.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential, because we can scale not only the model itself, but also the amount of computation we use when solving a problem. Instead of asking a model a question and getting one answer, you can let it try something, use a tool, observe the result, and revise its approach. Or you can have several agents explore different approaches and compare what they find.

But connecting more models doesn’t automatically make the system better. If they all make the same mistake, having ten of them agree is not very useful. The important question is how you organize the work and how you verify progress. With code, for example, you can run a test. That gives the agent feedback beyond another model saying, “Yes, this looks right.”

So I see a big opportunity in turning additional computation into longer, more reliable sequences of actions. The challenge is making sure that as you give the system more time and more agents, it actually solves harder problems, rather than just producing more conversation.

r001.rationale: The response expresses substantial potential from using more computation and multiple agents, but it does not communicate orders-of-magnitude scaling gains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential, but the important question is what you’re scaling. If you connect ten models and they all make the same mistake, you haven’t gained very much. You want them to do complementary work: explore different approaches, use tools, and check the results.

That gives you another dimension beyond the size of the model: how much computation you spend solving a problem. For a difficult task, an agent could try something, observe what happened, revise its plan, and keep going. You could also have several agents explore different solutions in parallel. But you need a way to identify which solution is actually better; otherwise, you’re just generating more text.

So I’m excited about that direction, especially for tasks where there’s feedback from the environment, like coding. The challenge is to train models to make productive use of those interactions. Simply putting models together is easy. Making the whole system reliably better as you give it more resources is the interesting part.

r001.rationale: The response describes substantial potential from agent systems and scaling computation with more resources, but it does not communicate orders-of-magnitude scaling gains.
